direction: Read this as the narrator of a gritty, smart short documentary. A grounded American man in his late forties, dry and observant, a little wry, never theatrical. Steady pace with brief beats at full stops.

lines.S1: April sixth, 1997. Athens, Ohio. Before the street ever filled up, police were already busy at the Crystal on Court Street, where about thirty members of Pi Kappa Alpha and Phi Kappa Tau had gone at each other with bottles, pool cues, pool balls and chairs. Not with cops. With each other.
lines.S2: Then the clocks sprang forward. Daylight saving time cut the night short by an hour, and about a thousand people, mostly O-U students, spilled onto North Court Street. One side chanted, tastes great. The other side answered, less filling. A broad, beer-soaked crowd, angry about last call. Not an ideological vanguard.
lines.S3: About seventy officers moved in. Trash cans burned. Bottles and eggs flew, and one officer went down, hit by a bottle. Four rounds of wooden pellets, the knee-knockers, went into the crowd. Yet nearly three decades on, the real story isn't the fire. It's the inversion.
lines.S4: In 1997, suburban Gen X frat culture wore its anti-authority streak like a badge. Part grunge cynicism, part Animal House, yelling at local cops about last call. Fast-forward thirty years, and that same demographic leans hard toward the police line, the property owners, and figures like Kyle Rittenhouse.
lines.S5: In ninety-seven, the campus story went easy on the crowd. The dean of students called it a far cry from a riot. The student paper settled on the word fracas. Students told of being shoved against cars. Today, plenty of that same cohort sees baton rounds and hard sweeps as plain order, when someone else is blocking the street.
lines.S6: Forty-seven people were arrested that night. Thirty-four were O-U students, charged with disorderly conduct, a misdemeanor. A year later, it happened again. Both nights get remembered as harmless fun, because a misdemeanor is the kind of charge that rarely follows anyone into a corporate job, or a cul-de-sac.
lines.S7: Sociologically, it isn't even a contradiction. It's territory. At twenty, Uptown Athens was their turf, and the cops were the outsiders. At fifty, homeowners and parents guard their own boundaries with the same entitlement.
lines.S8: At twenty, freedom meant throwing bottles when the bars closed early. At fifty, law and order means cheering the line.
lines.S9: Will we be remembered as the generation who raged against the machine, so long as the machine prevented more of our own consumption? Our generation winks and nods at the machine, when it stomps on the humanity of the less represented, and the less capitally secure.

chants.direction: Shout this like a rowdy college kid in a big crowd on a street at 2 AM, repeating it rhythmically, loud and slurred:

lines.great: Tastes great! Tastes great! Tastes great! Tastes great!
lines.less: Less filling! Less filling! Less filling! Less filling!
